title: Advanced Work Problems — Efficiency Variation
tagline: Year 3 — Efficiency ratios, workers who change speed, partial completion and man-hours

introduction.overview: Basic time-and-work problems add the rates of workers who work together. Advanced problems vary the efficiency: workers are compared by an efficiency ratio, work at a different speed after a break, are replaced by more or fewer workers part-way, or have different working hours per day. The method is to measure the work in units (for example LCM units) and to track how many units are done in each phase.
introduction.placementRelevance: Advanced work problems are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually with two or three phases and a ratio of efficiencies.
introduction.realWorldContext: Staffing a project, planning overtime and estimating completion when team size changes depend on these calculations.

learningObjectives: Use efficiency ratios to compare workers
Solve multi-phase problems with changing team size
Use man-hours with different hours per day
Handle workers of different efficiency leaving or joining
Find the completion time after a speed change

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Rate = work ÷ time. Efficiency is proportional to rate. Total work = rate × time summed over all phases.

coreDefinitions: Efficiency: the amount of work a worker does per unit time; efficiency ratio is the inverse of the time ratio.
Work units: a convenient total, usually the LCM of the given times.
Man-hours: workers × hours per day × days; constant for a given job with equal efficiency.
Phase: a period during which the team and rates stay the same.
Productivity change: a percentage change in a worker's rate.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Work is a quantity that accumulates in phases. Choose units so that every worker's daily output is a whole number, add the output of each phase, and stop when the total reaches the job size.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Take total work = LCM of the times. Write the units per day of each worker, add the phase outputs, subtract from the total and divide by the new rate.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Efficiency ratio
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: A : B = time of B : time of A

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Phase work
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: A alone 5 days then A + B

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Efficiency change
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: New time = old time × old rate ÷ new rate

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Replacement
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Units done so far, units left ÷ new rate
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: 20 men for 10 days of 30, then 5 leave

mainNarrative: Use LCM units. A takes 20 days and B takes 30, so take the job as 60 units: A does 3 units a day and B does 2. Together they do 5 units a day and finish in 12 days. A is 50% more efficient than B, matching the ratio 3 : 2.

For multi-phase problems, add the work of each phase. If A works alone for 5 days (15 units) and then A and B work together, the remaining 45 units take 9 days at 5 units a day, so the total is 14 days.

For changes in efficiency, scale the time. A worker who becomes 25% more efficient takes 4/5 of the original time. If 20 workers can finish a job in 30 days and after 10 days 5 workers leave, the remaining two-thirds of the work (400 of 600 man-days) is done by 15 workers in 400 ÷ 15 ≈ 26.7 days.
For man-hours, keep the product constant. 6 men working 9 hours a day complete a job in 10 days, which is 540 man-hours. 9 men working 5 hours a day need 540 ÷ 45 = 12 days.
For a worker whose rate changes, compute the output before and after the change separately. A worker who produces 10 units a day for 4 days and then 14 units a day does 40 + 14t after the change.

deepDiveAspects.title: Efficiency as a percentage
deepDiveAspects.content: If A is 25% more efficient than B, then A : B = 5 : 4 in rate and 4 : 5 in time. Convert percentages to ratios before computing.

deepDiveAspects.title: Idle days
deepDiveAspects.content: If a worker is absent on some days, subtract those days from his working time before computing his share of the work.

solvedExamples.title: Efficiency and units
solvedExamples.question: A can do a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. They work together; how long do they take, and how much more efficient is A than B?

steps.title: Units
steps.explanation: Total = 60 units. A does 3, B does 2 per day.

steps.title: Efficiency
steps.explanation: A : B = 3 : 2, so A is 50% more efficient.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Efficiency is inversely proportional to time.

solvedExamples.title: Team changes mid-job
solvedExamples.question: 20 workers can finish a job in 30 days. After 10 days, 5 workers leave. How many more days do the remaining workers need?
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using 20 workers for the remaining time.

solvedExamples.title: Hours per day
solvedExamples.question: 6 men working 9 hours a day complete a job in 10 days. In how many days will 9 men working 5 hours a day complete it?
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Ignoring the change in hours per day.

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Use fractions of work at every step.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Choose LCM units, list units per day, add the phases, and divide the remainder by the new rate.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the time ratio as the efficiency ratio
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Efficiency is the inverse of time.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using the full job for the second phase.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The completion time must lie between the times for the fastest and the slowest team.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write a phase table with units per day.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Multi-phase problems are two or three simple steps.

easy.question: A can do a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. Together they finish in (days)
A takes 10 days and B takes 15 days to do a job. The ratio of their efficiencies A : B is
easy.explanation: Efficiency is inversely proportional to time: 15 : 10 = 3 : 2.

easy.question: If A is twice as efficient as B and B alone takes 24 days, A alone takes (days)
easy.explanation: A takes half the time: 12 days.

intermediate.question: 6 men working 9 hours a day complete a job in 10 days. 9 men working 5 hours a day will take (days)
20 workers can finish a job in 30 days. After 10 days, 5 workers leave. The remaining workers need how many more days? (to one decimal place)
A can do a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. A starts, and after 5 days B joins. The total time is (days)
intermediate.explanation: A does 1/4 in 5 days. The remaining 3/4 at 1/12 per day takes 9 days. Total 14.

advanced.question: A and B can finish a job in 12 and 18 days. They work together for 4 days, then B leaves. A finishes the rest in (days)
advanced.explanation: In 4 days they do 4 × 5/36 = 5/9. Left 4/9 at A's rate 1/12: 16/3 = 5.33 days.

advanced.question: A can do a job in 10 days. B is 25% less efficient than A. They work together for 4 days. The fraction of the job left is
advanced.explanation: B's rate = 0.75 × 1/10 = 3/40. Together 7/40 per day. In 4 days 28/40 = 7/10 is done, so 3/10 is left.

placementStyle.question: Efficiencies of A, B and C are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. A alone takes 30 days. All three together take (days)
placementStyle.explanation: Rates 2, 3, 5 units; A's 2 units take 30 days so total job = 60 units. Together 10 units a day: 6 days.

placementStyle.question: 20 men were to finish a job in 40 days. After 10 days, 10 more men joined. The job finished in how many days from the start?
placementStyle.explanation: Total 800 man-days. After 10 days 600 remain. 30 men take 20 days. Total 30.

placementStyle.question: A takes 24 days and B takes 36 days to do a job. They work on alternate days, starting with A. The job is finished in (days)
placementStyle.explanation: A + B pair does 1/24 + 1/36 = 5/72 per two days. After 28 days (14 pairs) 70/72 is done. A then does 3/72 on day 29, completing the job.
